questions.question: Kafka Streams vs Flink vs Spark Streaming — how do you pick a stream processing framework?
questions.title: Stream Processing: Kafka Streams vs Flink vs Spark Structured Streaming
questions.direct_answer: Three dominant real-time stream processors, each with different sweet spots: **Kafka Streams** is a Java library (no cluster, runs inside your app) — best for Kafka-centric, embeddable processing with stateful operations (joins, aggregations, windowing); limited to Kafka as source/sink. **Apache Flink** is a dedicated stream engine with true event-time processing, low latency (sub-second), rich state management, and checkpoint-based exactly-once — best for complex stateful pipelines, CEP, and heavy windowing. **Spark Structured Streaming** extends Spark's batch model to streams (micro-batches) — best when you already use Spark for batch, want unified code, and sub-second latency isn't required. Rule of thumb: Kafka Streams for simple Kafka → Kafka topologies embedded in apps; Flink for serious stateful streaming; Spark when you're already on Spark.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of modern stream processing, event-time semantics, and framework trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing stream processing with message queues; ignoring event-time vs processing-time; thinking Spark Streaming is real real-time
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss event time vs processing time, watermarks, exactly-once semantics, state backends, checkpointing, windowing types, and operational cost

sections.title: Why Stream Processing, and the Three Contenders
sections.content:
Stream processing transforms real-time data as it arrives — filter, enrich, aggregate, join — producing new streams. Unlike batch (process a bounded dataset), streams are unbounded; the framework must handle state, out-of-order events, failures, and time.

**Kafka Streams** — a Java library from Confluent/Apache.
- You embed it in your Spring Boot or plain Java app; no separate cluster.
- Reads from Kafka topics, writes to Kafka topics.
- Supports windowed aggregations, joins (stream-stream, stream-table), interactive queries (query state from REST API).
- State stored in embedded RocksDB; backed up to Kafka internal topics.
- Exactly-once via transactional producer.
- Perfect when your data is already in Kafka and the processing topology is moderate complexity.

**Apache Flink** — the state-of-the-art streaming engine.
- Native event-time processing, watermarks, true exactly-once via distributed snapshots (Chandy-Lamport algorithm). Low latency (sub-second, often ms).
- Rich windowing (tumbling, sliding, session, custom).
- State backends: RocksDB on local disk or in-memory, checkpointed to S3/HDFS.
- Complex Event Processing (CEP) library for pattern matching.
- Dedicated cluster (JobManager + TaskManagers).
- Used by Uber, Netflix, Alibaba, LinkedIn at scale.

**Spark Structured Streaming** — evolution of Spark Streaming (DStreams).
- Treats a stream as an unbounded table, incrementally appended.
- Micro-batch execution by default (seconds latency); continuous mode for ms latency but limited operations.
- Rich ecosystem with Spark SQL, MLlib, batch integration.
- Best when you already run Spark for batch and want unified code.

**Other options:** Apache Beam (portable API, runs on Flink/Spark/Dataflow); Google Dataflow (managed Beam on GCP); AWS Kinesis Data Analytics (managed Flink); Apache Pulsar Functions (stream processing in Pulsar). Kafka + Flink is the popular 2026 combo.

sections.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
sections.content:
| Dimension | Kafka Streams | Flink | Spark Structured Streaming |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Deployment model** | Library in app | Dedicated cluster | Dedicated Spark cluster |
| **Latency** | Low (~10ms) | Very low (ms–sub-s) | Medium (seconds in micro-batch, ms in continuous) |
| **Processing model** | True streaming | True streaming | Micro-batch (default), continuous (limited) |
| **Sources / sinks** | Kafka only (officially) | Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar, files, DBs, etc. | Rich: Kafka, files, Delta Lake, JDBC |
| **Event-time processing** | Yes | Best in class | Yes (v3+) |
| **Watermarks** | Yes | First-class, flexible | Yes |
| **State management** | RocksDB, changelog | RocksDB/heap, checkpoints | State store, checkpoints |
| **Exactly-once** | Yes (within Kafka) | Yes (end-to-end with transactional sinks) | Yes (with transactional sinks) |
| **Windowing** | Tumbling, sliding, session, hopping | Tumbling, sliding, session, global, custom | Tumbling, sliding, session |
| **Joins** | Stream-stream, stream-table | All types including temporal | All types |
| **Operational complexity** | Low (embedded) | High (cluster) | Medium (Spark-native) |
| **Scaling model** | App instances (consumer group) | Parallel tasks on TaskManagers | Executors on cluster |
| **Typical use cases** | Event-driven microservices, enrichment, aggregations | Complex event processing, fraud detection, real-time analytics, heavy state | ETL, ML on streams, Spark-shop real-time |
| **Learning curve** | Moderate (Kafka + DSL) | Steep (concepts + cluster) | Moderate (if Spark-savvy) |

sections.title: Concrete Examples and Decision Framework
sections.content:
**Kafka Streams example — real-time order aggregation**

```java
@Configuration
@EnableKafkaStreams
public class OrderStreamsConfig {

    @Bean
    public KStream<String, Order> orderStream(StreamsBuilder builder) {
        KStream<String, Order> orders = builder.stream(
            "orders",
            Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), new JsonSerde<>(Order.class)));

        orders
            .filter((k, o) -> o.getStatus() == PLACED)
            .groupBy((k, o) -> o.getCustomerId())
            .windowedBy(TimeWindows.of(Duration.ofMinutes(5)))
            .aggregate(
                CustomerWindow::new,
                (key, order, window) -> window.add(order),
                Materialized.with(Serdes.String(), new JsonSerde<>(CustomerWindow.class)))
            .toStream()
            .to("customer-5min-aggregates");

        return orders;
    }
}
```

Runs inside your Spring Boot app. Scales by running multiple app instances (same consumer group). State in RocksDB locally.

**Flink example — fraud detection with CEP**

```java
StreamExecutionEnvironment env = StreamExecutionEnvironment.getExecutionEnvironment();
env.enableCheckpointing(60_000);  // checkpoint every 60s
env.setStateBackend(new EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend());
env.getCheckpointConfig().setCheckpointStorage("s3://my-flink-checkpoints/");

DataStream<Transaction> transactions = env.fromSource(
    KafkaSource.<Transaction>builder()
        .setBootstrapServers("broker:9092")
        .setTopics("transactions")
        .setValueOnlyDeserializer(new TransactionDeserializer())
        .build(),
    WatermarkStrategy.<Transaction>forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
        .withTimestampAssigner((t, ts) -> t.getEventTime().toEpochMilli()),
    "kafka-source");

// Pattern: small txn followed by large txn within 1 minute
Pattern<Transaction, ?> fraudPattern = Pattern
    .<Transaction>begin("small").where(new SimpleCondition<>() {
        @Override public boolean filter(Transaction t) { return t.getAmount().compareTo(BigDecimal.ONE) < 0; }
    })
    .next("large").where(new SimpleCondition<>() {
        @Override public boolean filter(Transaction t) { return t.getAmount().compareTo(new BigDecimal(500)) > 0; }
    })
    .within(Time.minutes(1));

CEP.pattern(transactions.keyBy(Transaction::getCardId), fraudPattern)
    .select((Map<String, List<Transaction>> pattern) -> {
        return new FraudAlert(pattern.get("large").get(0));
    })
    .sinkTo(KafkaSink.<FraudAlert>builder()
        .setBootstrapServers("broker:9092")
        .setRecordSerializer(KafkaRecordSerializationSchema.builder()
            .setTopic("fraud-alerts")
            .setValueSerializationSchema(new FraudAlertSerializer())
            .build())
        .build());

env.execute("Fraud Detection");
```

Dedicated Flink cluster; TaskManagers run the tasks; checkpoints to S3 for recovery.

**Spark Structured Streaming example — ETL to Delta Lake**

```scala
val stream = spark.readStream
  .format("kafka")
  .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker:9092")
  .option("subscribe", "events")
  .load()
  .selectExpr("CAST(value AS STRING) as json")
  .select(from_json($"json", schema).as("data"))
  .select("data.*")

stream
  .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
  .groupBy(window($"event_time", "5 minutes"), $"user_id")
  .agg(count("*").as("event_count"))
  .writeStream
  .format("delta")
  .outputMode("append")
  .option("checkpointLocation", "s3://checkpoints/user-activity")
  .toTable("user_activity_5min")
```

Runs on existing Spark cluster; writes to Delta Lake table; unified with batch Spark jobs.

**Decision framework:**

*Pick Kafka Streams when:*
- Data is in Kafka, output goes to Kafka
- Processing is embedded in a microservice
- State requirements moderate (RocksDB fits on local SSD)
- Team wants library simplicity, not cluster ops
- Typical: event enrichment, real-time aggregations in Spring Boot apps

*Pick Flink when:*
- Complex stateful processing (huge state, complex windowing)
- Event-time semantics matter (lots of out-of-order data)
- Sub-second latency required
- Heterogeneous sources: Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar, files
- Team has engineering capacity for cluster ops
- Typical: fraud detection, real-time analytics, CEP, large-scale enrichment pipelines

*Pick Spark Structured Streaming when:*
- Already running Spark for batch; want unified code
- Latency needs are seconds, not ms
- Data lake integration (Delta Lake, Iceberg, Hudi)
- ML inference on streams (MLlib / MLflow)
- Typical: streaming ETL into data lake, ML feature updates

sections.title: Trade-offs and Key Concepts
sections.content:
**Event time vs processing time.** Events have timestamps (event time) but arrive at the processor later (processing time).
- A 5-minute window on event time must wait for late-arriving events.
- Watermarks mark 'we believe all events up to time T have arrived'; late events trigger specific handling.
- Flink has best event-time support; Kafka Streams and Spark are good.

**Watermarks.** Signal event-time progress. 'Watermark at T=12:05' means window for 12:00–12:05 can close. Late events may be dropped or routed to side output. Tuning watermark lag is critical — too low, drops correct events; too high, adds latency.

**State management.** - **Kafka Streams**: RocksDB on local disk; state changes logged to a Kafka changelog topic for recovery.
- On restart, rebuilds state by replaying changelog.
- Slow for huge state.
- **Flink**: RocksDB or heap. Incremental checkpoints to S3/HDFS.
- Can restore from any checkpoint; supports savepoints (manual, versioned checkpoints for upgrades).
- **Spark**: RocksDB-backed state store. Checkpoints to HDFS/S3.

**Exactly-once semantics.**
- **Kafka Streams**: exactly-once within Kafka (read-process-write atomic via transactions).
- **Flink**: end-to-end exactly-once when sinks support transactions (Kafka, JDBC with XA, Iceberg).
- **Spark**: exactly-once with transactional sinks.

None extend exactly-once automatically to arbitrary external systems (REST calls, non-transactional DBs). Idempotent sinks or dedup downstream is still required.

**Checkpointing frequency.**
- Too frequent: overhead (IO, snapshot cost)
- Too rare: large re-processing on failure
- Flink typical: 1–10 minutes; Kafka Streams commits offsets every 30s by default

**Backpressure.**
- **Flink**: native backpressure via buffer-based flow control; slow sinks slow upstream.
- **Kafka Streams**: naturally backpressure via Kafka consumer pull.
- **Spark**: rate limiting via `maxOffsetsPerTrigger`.

**Scaling.**
- **Kafka Streams**: add app instances (same consumer group); Kafka partitions assigned.
- **Flink**: change parallelism; rescaling requires savepoint + restore.
- **Spark**: add executors; dynamic allocation supported.

**Testing.**
- Kafka Streams: TopologyTestDriver, no cluster needed
- Flink: MiniCluster for integration tests
- Spark: local mode

**Operational cost.**
- **Kafka Streams**: no extra infrastructure; just apps
- **Flink**: dedicated cluster (JobManager HA, TaskManagers), non-trivial to run
- **Spark**: Spark cluster (Standalone, YARN, Kubernetes); DIY complexity

**Latency regimes.**
- **Sub-10ms**: Flink
- **10–100ms**: Kafka Streams, Flink
- **Seconds**: Spark micro-batch

**Unified batch + streaming (Beam / Spark).** If you want same code for bounded and unbounded data, Beam (Google's unified model) or Spark (which already supports both) wins. Flink supports batch via the same API but is streaming-first.

**Windowing types.**
- **Tumbling**: non-overlapping fixed windows (every 5 min)
- **Sliding**: overlapping fixed windows (every 5 min, advancing every 1 min)
- **Session**: gap-based (events within 30s of each other = same session)
- **Global**: single window, custom triggers

Flink has the richest windowing semantics; the others cover common cases.

**Joins.**
- **Stream-stream**: KafkaStreams (time-windowed), Flink (time-windowed + interval)
- **Stream-table**: KafkaStreams KTable, Flink Table API, Spark static DataFrame
- **Temporal joins**: Flink excels; valuable for 'at transaction time, look up exchange rate'

**Schema evolution.** With Avro/Protobuf + Schema Registry, compatible changes don't require restart. Breaking changes require savepoint + code upgrade + restore.

**The default recommendation in 2026:**
- **Embedded simple streaming in Spring Boot**: Kafka Streams
- **Complex real-time pipelines with heavy state**: Flink
- **Already on Spark, seconds latency OK**: Spark Structured Streaming
- **Multi-cloud portable**: Beam on Dataflow or Flink
- **On AWS, don't want ops**: Kinesis Data Analytics (managed Flink) or MSK + Kafka Streams

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Three dominant frameworks**, each optimized for different scenarios
- **Kafka Streams**: library in your app, Kafka → Kafka, moderate complexity; no cluster
- **Flink**: dedicated cluster, true streaming, best event-time and exactly-once, handles massive state
- **Spark Structured Streaming**: micro-batch + continuous mode, best when already on Spark; latency in seconds
- **Event time vs processing time** is fundamental — watermarks signal event-time progress
- **Exactly-once is within the system** — extending to external non-transactional systems needs idempotency
- **State backends** matter — RocksDB + checkpoints to S3/HDFS for recovery
- **Kafka Streams scales via app instances**; Flink via parallelism; Spark via executors
- **Windowing types**: tumbling, sliding, session, global; Flink richest semantics
- **Pick based on latency, state size, existing ecosystem, team ops capacity**

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Stream processing transforms real-time data as it arrives: filter, enrich, aggregate, join. Unlike batch, streams are unbounded, so the framework must handle state, out-of-order events, failures, and time itself.

Three dominant frameworks in 2026.

**Kafka Streams**
- A Java library, not a cluster
- Embedded in your Spring Boot or plain Java app
- Reads from Kafka topics, writes to Kafka topics
- Supports windowed aggregations, joins, interactive queries
- State in embedded RocksDB; backed up to Kafka changelog topic
- Exactly-once via Kafka transactions
- Scales by running multiple app instances (consumer group)
- Perfect for Kafka-centric processing inside microservices

**Apache Flink**
- State-of-the-art streaming engine
- Dedicated cluster: JobManager plus TaskManagers
- Native event-time processing; watermarks are first-class
- True exactly-once via distributed snapshots (Chandy-Lamport)
- Sub-second to millisecond latency
- Rich windowing: tumbling, sliding, session, global, custom
- State backends: RocksDB on local disk, incremental checkpoints to S3
- Complex Event Processing (CEP) library for pattern matching
- Used by Uber, Netflix, Alibaba, LinkedIn at scale

**Spark Structured Streaming**
- Evolution of Spark Streaming (DStreams)
- Treats stream as unbounded table incrementally appended
- Micro-batch execution by default (seconds latency)
- Continuous mode for milliseconds but limited operations
- Rich ecosystem: Spark SQL, MLlib, batch integration
- Best when you already run Spark and want unified code

**Key concepts to explain**

*Event time vs processing time*
- Events have timestamps (event time); arrive at processor later (processing time)
- A 5-minute window on event time must wait for late events
- Watermarks mark 'all events up to time T have arrived'
- Flink has best event-time support

*Watermarks*
- Signal event-time progress
- Too low: drops correct events; too high: adds latency
- Tune based on observed lag distribution

*State management*
- Kafka Streams: RocksDB locally; changelog topic for recovery
- Flink: RocksDB, incremental checkpoints to S3; savepoints for upgrades
- Spark: state store, checkpoints to HDFS/S3

*Exactly-once*
- Within Kafka: Kafka Streams and Flink both support via transactions
- End-to-end: Flink with transactional sinks (Kafka, JDBC XA, Iceberg)
- External non-transactional systems: still need idempotent sinks or dedupe

**When to pick each**

*Pick Kafka Streams when*
- Data already in Kafka, output to Kafka
- Embedded in a microservice
- Moderate state (fits on local SSD)
- No cluster ops capacity; simple is good
- Typical: event enrichment, real-time aggregations in Spring Boot

*Pick Flink when*
- Complex stateful processing with huge state
- Event-time semantics critical; lots of out-of-order data
- Sub-second latency required
- Heterogeneous sources: Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar, files
- Team has engineering capacity for cluster ops
- Typical: fraud detection, real-time analytics, CEP

*Pick Spark Structured Streaming when*
- Already running Spark for batch; unified code wins
- Latency needs are seconds, not milliseconds
- Data lake integration: Delta Lake, Iceberg, Hudi
- ML inference on streams via MLlib or MLflow
- Typical: streaming ETL into data lake

**Operational trade-offs**
- Kafka Streams: no extra infrastructure; just apps
- Flink: dedicated cluster with HA JobManager; non-trivial ops
- Spark: Spark cluster; DIY complexity

**Latency regimes**
- Sub-10ms: Flink
- 10–100ms: Kafka Streams, Flink
- Seconds: Spark micro-batch

**Scaling models**
- Kafka Streams: add app instances; consumer group assigns partitions
- Flink: change parallelism; rescaling via savepoint plus restore
- Spark: add executors; dynamic allocation supported

**Windowing types**
- Tumbling: non-overlapping fixed (every 5 minutes)
- Sliding: overlapping fixed (every 5 minutes, sliding every 1 minute)
- Session: gap-based (events within 30 seconds of each other)
- Global: single window with custom triggers
- Flink richest; Kafka Streams and Spark cover common cases

**Unified batch and streaming**
- Beam (Google's unified model) runs on Flink, Spark, Dataflow
- Spark natively unified batch and streaming
- Flink is streaming-first but supports batch

**Managed options**
- AWS Kinesis Data Analytics: managed Flink
- Confluent Cloud: managed Kafka + ksqlDB (SQL on Kafka Streams)
- Databricks: managed Spark
- Google Dataflow: managed Beam

**The strategic answer**
- Kafka Streams for embedded simple streaming in microservices
- Flink for serious stateful streaming at scale
- Spark Structured Streaming when already on Spark
- Event-time semantics and exactly-once are non-negotiable for correctness
- Operational cost often the deciding factor — managed options shift the calculus

questions.question: What's the difference between KStream, KTable, and GlobalKTable in Kafka Streams?
questions.title: Kafka Streams: KStream vs KTable vs GlobalKTable
questions.direct_answer: **KStream** models a Kafka topic as an unbounded sequence of independent records — each record is a fact (e.g. 'user clicked X at time T'). **KTable** models the same topic as a **changelog**: each record is the latest value for its key, conceptually a row in a continuously updated table (built on a compacted topic). **GlobalKTable** is a KTable replicated **fully to every Streams instance** instead of partitioned, used for broadcast lookups against small reference data. KStream is for events; KTable is for current state per key; GlobalKTable is for small lookup tables that every task needs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand stream-table duality and can pick the right abstraction for events vs current-state vs broadcast lookups
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using KStream for what's really a stateful per-key view and ending up reimplementing aggregation, or using GlobalKTable for large datasets where memory blows up on every instance
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain stream-table duality, windowed aggregations (tumbling/hopping/session), state stores backed by compacted topics, and the partitioning requirements for KStream-KTable joins

sections.title: Stream-Table Duality: Three Ways to View the Same Topic
sections.content:
A Kafka topic is just a sequence of `(key, value)` records. Kafka Streams gives you three different abstractions over that same data, and choosing the right one is the most important design decision in any Streams app.

**`KStream<K,V>`** treats the topic as a stream of independent facts.
- Every record is appended to the conceptual log; nothing replaces anything. `clicks`, `payments`, `page-views`, `orders-placed` — events that happened.
- Operations on a KStream produce new records: `mapValues` transforms each one, `filter` drops some, `flatMap` produces multiple.
- Aggregations explicitly add windowing because there is no implicit current state per key.

**`KTable<K,V>`** treats the topic as a **changelog**: each record updates the latest value for its key.
- Conceptually it's a table where the row for `userId=42` is whatever the most recent record with key 42 said.
- KTable operations work on the latest-per-key view: `filter` is on the current row, `mapValues` transforms the current value, joins use the current value for the key.
- Under the hood, every KTable is backed by a local **state store** (RocksDB by default) replicated by a compacted Kafka topic, so each instance can answer point lookups by key without going to the broker.

**`GlobalKTable<K,V>`** is a KTable that is **fully replicated to every Kafka Streams instance** rather than partitioned across them.
- Useful for broadcast lookups against small reference data — country codes, product catalogs, user-tier tables — where you need to enrich a stream by an arbitrary key that doesn't match the stream's partitioning.
- The cost is that every instance holds the full dataset in its local state store, so you only use it when 'small' is genuinely small (typically tens of MB to a few GB total).

The duality is concrete: `KStream.toTable()` turns a stream into a table by treating each record as the latest value, and `KTable.toStream()` turns a table back into a stream of changes. You move between the two views as the processing topology requires.

sections.title: Windowing: Tumbling, Hopping, Session
sections.content:
KStream aggregations require windowing — you have to tell Streams over what time slice to compute the result. Three window types cover almost all use cases.

**Tumbling windows** are non-overlapping fixed-size buckets: `TimeWindows.of(Duration.ofMinutes(5))` produces results for `[00:00, 00:05)`, `[00:05, 00:10)`, and so on.
- Every record falls into exactly one window.
- Use for hourly or daily counts, billing aggregates, and any reporting where buckets must not overlap.

**Hopping windows** are fixed-size and overlap by a hop interval: `TimeWindows.of(Duration.ofMinutes(5)).advanceBy(Duration.ofMinutes(1))` produces a 5-minute window every 1 minute.
- Each record lands in 5 windows simultaneously.
- Use for moving-average dashboards and trend detection where you want a smooth rolling metric instead of stair-step buckets.

**Session windows** are activity-driven: `SessionWindows.ofInactivityGapWithNoGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(30))` groups records by key into a session that ends when no record arrives for the gap. Use for user-session analytics, IoT device sessions, and any scenario where the meaningful boundary is 'period of activity' rather than wall-clock time.

**Late-arriving records** are the operational gotcha.
- By default Streams accepts records up to `grace.ms` past the window end, after which they're dropped.
- Set the grace period explicitly based on your producer's worst-case lateness — analytics topics often need 10-60 minutes of grace; metrics topics with reliable ingestion need only seconds.
- Records that arrive past the grace period silently disappear from window aggregations, which is rarely what users expect.

sections.title: Spring Kafka Streams Binder: KStream + KTable + GlobalKTable
Co-partitioning, State Stores, and the Common Production Gotchas
sections.content:
**KStream-KTable joins require co-partitioning.** Both inputs must have the same number of partitions and use the same key serializer/partitioner.
- If `clicks` has 12 partitions and `users` has 6, the join silently produces wrong results.
- Streams does not enforce this — it's your job to ensure topics are co-partitioned at creation.
- When the keys match but the partitioning doesn't, repartition explicitly with `selectKey().groupByKey()` before joining.

**KStream-GlobalKTable joins do NOT require co-partitioning.** That's the whole point — you can look up by any field of the stream record, not just the stream's key.
- The price is that every instance holds the full GlobalKTable in its local state store.
- A 100-MB country reference table replicated across 20 Streams instances costs 2 GB of memory total but trivializes the lookup; a 50-GB user table doing the same would be a disaster.

**State stores are RocksDB by default**, persisted to local disk and backed by a compacted Kafka topic (`changelog topic`).
- On restart, Streams restores the state store by reading the changelog topic from the beginning.
- For large state stores this restore can take many minutes — set `num.standby.replicas >= 1` so a hot standby instance has the state pre-loaded and can take over immediately during failover.

**Watch out for `processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2`** — it gives you transactional read-process-write across input topic, output topic, and state-store changelog, but it requires `replication.factor=3` on internal topics and adds noticeable latency. Use it when correctness matters (financial aggregates, billing) and stick with the default `at_least_once` for analytics where occasional duplicates are acceptable.

**Punctuators and wall-clock vs event-time** are easy to misconfigure.
- Streams defaults to event-time semantics — the timestamp embedded in each record.
- If your producers don't set timestamps explicitly, they get the producer's wall clock, which causes confusing behavior when records are produced in batches or replayed.
- Configure `default.timestamp.extractor` explicitly to make event-time deterministic.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **KStream is for facts; KTable is for current state per key; GlobalKTable is for broadcast lookups.**
- **`KStream.toTable()` and `KTable.toStream()`** capture stream-table duality — move between them freely as the topology requires.
- **Windowing — tumbling for buckets, hopping for moving averages, session for activity-based.** Set `grace.ms` explicitly for late records.
- **KStream-KTable joins require co-partitioning** — same partition count and partitioner; KStream-GlobalKTable joins do not.
- **State stores are RocksDB backed by a compacted changelog topic** — set `num.standby.replicas >= 1` to avoid long restore times on failover.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Kafka Streams gives you three abstractions over the same topic, and the right choice depends on what each record means.

**KStream:**
- Treats records as immutable facts — clicks, payments, orders-placed
- Operations like `map`, `filter`, `flatMap` produce new records; aggregations require explicit windowing because there's no implicit per-key state

**KTable:**
- Treats the topic as a changelog — each record is the latest value for its key, conceptually a table row
- Backed by a local RocksDB state store and a compacted changelog topic, so point lookups by key are local
- Use it for current state per key like user profiles or account balances

**GlobalKTable:**
- A KTable that's fully replicated to every Streams instance instead of partitioned
- Use it for small reference data — country codes, product catalogs — where any task might need to look up by an arbitrary field of the input record
- The cost is memory: every instance holds the full dataset, so it has to genuinely be small

**Windowing:**
- Tumbling — non-overlapping fixed buckets, for hourly or daily counts
- Hopping — fixed size with overlap, for moving-average dashboards
- Session — activity-driven, for user sessions and IoT bursts
- Always set `grace.ms` explicitly for late records, otherwise they silently disappear from aggregations

**Production gotchas:**
- KStream-KTable joins require co-partitioning — same partition count and partitioner — and Streams doesn't enforce it; KStream-GlobalKTable joins don't
- Set `num.standby.replicas >= 1` so failover doesn't trigger a multi-minute state-store restore from the changelog topic
- `processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2` is correct but slower; default `at_least_once` is fine for analytics

In Spring Boot the cleanest way to wire this is the Spring Cloud Stream Kafka Streams binder — declare the topology as a `Function<KStream, ...>` bean and configure inputs, outputs, and processing guarantees via application properties.
